Volume 10 · Chapter 05

Forwards, futures and swaps

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v10-c04

By the endDerive contract values and explain financing, collateral and basis effects.

Value the agreement and fund every payment

Capability. Derive forward delivery prices and existing contract values, reconstruct futures variation and financing cash, value fixed-for-floating swaps, and identify the assumptions behind carry, collateral and basis calculations. The prerequisite is credit risk and recovery; we use the dated discount factors of Chapter 1, the finite pricing laws of Chapter 3, and elementary conditional expectation. Continuous-time option pricing is not assumed.

Larch Treasury promises to deliver an asset in one year. Its trader says the forward “costs 103.20,” its valuation report says “value zero,” and its treasurer asks for cash to meet collateral calls. These statements can all be consistent. A delivery price is an amount exchanged later. A contract value is the price of the remaining rights and obligations now. A funding requirement is cash that must be available on a specified date. Confusing them produces apparently profitable strategies that cannot meet their payments.

All amounts below are original synthetic examples, expressed in fictional currency units (CU) unless foreign units (FU) are specified. Time is in years for discounting; margin dates can instead denote any three consecutive stipulated settlement intervals. There are no taxes, fees, delivery options or defaults unless introduced. No numerical input is a current market observation or exchange requirement. A contract's actual specification must determine its delivery asset, quantity, fixing, settlement dates, quotation, collateral and closeout rules.

1. The contract comes before the formula

Prices, values and quantities used in this chapter
SymbolMeaning and units
StSpot price at t, CU per asset unit; for FX, domestic CU per FU
D(t,T)Price at t of one default-free CU paid at T; positive, with D(t,t) = 1
KFixed delivery price on an existing forward, CU per unit
F(t,T)Delivery price making a newly entered forward have zero value
vt(K)Value at t of the old long forward per underlying unit
GiFutures settlement quotation at settlement date i
N, αi, kSwap notional in CU, accrual year fraction, fixed annual rate

A long physical forward receives one asset and pays K at T; after an immediate sale of the received asset its net cash is ST − K. A short has the opposite obligations. Cash settlement gives this difference directly only if the specified fixing corresponds to the same asset price. For N units multiply both price-dependent cash and value by N. A zero initial value does not mean the payoff is zero or the exposure is small. Unlike an option holder, the forward holder cannot simply decline an unfavorable exchange.

Distinguish initial payment from notional. A new fair forward ordinarily has no purchase premium in this frictionless model, but it may require collateral. Conversely, an old forward can be transferred for a nonzero amount while keeping K unchanged. An agreement with a deliberately off-market K needs an offsetting upfront payment to be fair. The distinction follows by comparing its terminal cash with that of a new zero-value contract.

2. Carry pricing by dated replication

Suppose one unit can be bought, held and delivered. Before T it pays known income Ij and requires known holding costs Cj at dates tj. Their present values are I = ΣIjD(0,tj) and U = ΣCjD(0,tj). Let A = S0 + U − I. Under the replication rights below, A is the prepaid cost of receiving one unit at T with no intervening net payments.

F(0,T) = A / D(0,T).
v0(K) = A − KD(0,T) = D(0,T)[F(0,T) − K].

Derivation. Buy one asset. For each net income Ij − Cj, borrow its discounted amount now and repay that net receipt on date tj. A negative net receipt instead requires purchasing a dated cash claim to cover the cost. The resulting portfolio costs A now, has zero interim net cash, and delivers one asset at T. Combining it with borrowing A due at T costs zero and leaves one asset against a repayment A/D(0,T). Selling a forward above this repayment creates a positive known terminal surplus. If all the component positions can be reversed on the same terms, buying a forward below this amount and reversing the portfolio also creates a surplus. No arbitrage therefore pins down F. Subtracting a T-dated liability K gives the value of any old long contract.

The proof needs enforceable income and delivery rights, matched dates, unrestricted lending and borrowing on the specified curve, and executable asset and forward trades. The reverse direction additionally needs asset borrowing and the ability to reverse the full carry package at its stated cost. With a commodity, physical storage purchased by an owner is not automatically a service that a short seller can sell back. When that reverse strategy is unavailable, cash-and-carry may establish only an upper bound, even if storage costs are known. A short-sale fee, recall risk, delivery grade mismatch or inability to fund a margin call breaks a claimed unrestricted arbitrage unless it is explicitly included.

At a later valuation date t, include only payments still belonging to the holder after t. Use the current spot price, the current discount curve and the remaining income/cost rights to form At; then vt(K) = At − KD(t,T). Do not replace the contractual K with the new F(t,T), which would value a different agreement. At maturity, with delivery costs and payouts consistently allocated, D(T,T) = 1 and vT = ST − K. Positive discounts can exceed one under negative rates; the argument never requires a positive yield.

Worked example 1 — A forward is not purchased for its delivery price

An asset costs 100 now, pays 3 after half a year and requires a contractual holding payment of 1 on that same date. D(0,0.5) = 0.98 and D(0,1) = 0.95. Assume the entire carry package is reversible. Its net half-year receipt is 2, so A = 100 − 2(0.98) = 98.04. The fair delivery price is 98.04/0.95 = 103.20. An old long forward with K = 101 has value 98.04 − 101(0.95) = 2.09.

For the actual financing ledger, borrow 1.96 now against repayment 2 at the half-year date, and borrow 98.04 against repayment 103.20 at year one. The 100 of borrowing purchases the asset. The half-year dividend, storage expense and debt repayment net to 3 − 1 − 2 = 0. If a zero-upfront forward can be sold at K = 106, deliver the asset at year one, collect 106 and repay 103.20: the terminal surplus is 2.80. Every date is funded. Its current value is 2.80(0.95) = 2.66.

Immediately after the half-year receipts, suppose spot is 108, there are no remaining holding payments, and D(0.5,1) = 0.98. The old K = 101 long is now worth 108 − 101(0.98) = 9.02. The new fair delivery price is 108/0.98 ≈ 110.204082, but the old contract still requires 101 at delivery.

For a tradable asset paying a deterministic proportional dividend yield q, reinvestment changes the number of shares. With continuous reinvestment and no tax or dealing cost, n′(t) = qn(t), so buying e−qT shares now grows to one share at T. Its prepaid delivery cost is S0e−qT. With a constant continuously compounded funding rate r, F = S0e(r−q)T. This argument uses an ordinary differential equation for share accumulation, not a forecast of the share price. A fixed cash dividend is a different contract and belongs in the dated-income formula. An uncertain dividend is neither a known cash strip nor a deterministic q merely because an analyst supplies its mean.

In a commodity market, a quoted convenience yield can parameterize the advantage of possessing available inventory. Writing F = S e(r+u−y)T with storage rate u and residual yield y is a specified representation, not proof that inventory services can be borrowed or sold. Without those trading rights, solving the equation for y does not create an independently observed tradable cash income.

3. Currency forwards and the executable funding test

Let S quote domestic currency per foreign unit. To own one FU at T, buy Df(0,T) FU today and invest it in the foreign cash account. Its domestic cost is SDf. Financing this purchase in domestic currency costs SDf/Dd at T. With matched default-free funding rights, currency convertibility and symmetric executable trades,

Fd/f(0,T) = Sd/fDf(0,T) / Dd(0,T).
vlong = Nf[SDf − KDd].

This is covered interest parity in the specified frictionless setting. “Covered” means that the terminal currency conversion is contracted. It does not remove default, collateral, access or settlement mismatches. Reversing the quote requires reversing the underlying unit and notional consistently; simply swapping interest rates while keeping the old domestic-per-foreign quote is a units error.

Worked example 2 — Compare an apparent FX gain with actual funding

S = 1.20 CU/FU, Dd = 0.96, and Df = 0.99. A forward covers 2,000,000 FU. Buy 1,980,000 FU now for 2,376,000 CU; the foreign investment becomes 2,000,000 FU at maturity. Borrowing the domestic cost on the quoted curve requires repayment 2,475,000 CU. Hence F = 1.2375 CU/FU.

If Larch can sell the forward at 1.25 with zero upfront payment, delivery brings 2,500,000 CU and leaves 25,000 CU after the stated funding repayment. The long side of that off-market contract is worth −25,000(0.96) = −24,000 CU. Both signs are measured from the named position, not from an ambiguous statement that the “forward gains.”

Now suppose the same trader can borrow domestic funds only at gross 1.08 while the foreign investment still returns the stipulated amount. Repayment becomes 2,376,000(1.08) = 2,566,080 CU. Selling at 1.25 now loses 66,080 CU on that strategy. The cash-and-carry threshold is 1.28304, not 1.2375. This does not establish a universal fair quote; it shows why a benchmark-curve discrepancy is insufficient evidence of executable arbitrage.

With bid/ask quotations and distinct lending and borrowing gross factors, two sufficient arbitrage tests use different sides. Buying foreign currency at Sask, lending it at Rf,lend and borrowing domestically at Rd,borrow gives an upper threshold SaskRd,borrow/Rf,lend; an executable forward bid above it permits the first trade before other costs. Borrowing foreign at Rf,borrow, selling it at Sbid, lending domestic at Rd,lend and buying foreign forward gives a lower threshold SbidRd,lend/Rf,borrow; a forward ask below it permits the reverse trade. A quote inside these thresholds is not an arbitrage identified by either strategy.

The dated BIS September 2016 study of cross-currency basis examines how hedging demand and balance-sheet constraints can accompany deviations from benchmark parity. We use that historical mechanism and its need for an executable funding comparison. Its empirical period is not evidence of today's basis, and a measured deviation alone does not identify one causal friction.

4. Futures settle cash before final delivery

For a simple linear futures quotation, a position of n contracts with multiplier m CU per quoted unit receives variation n m(Gi − Gi−1) at settlement i. Positive n is long. For a fixed position the undiscounted variations telescope to nm(GM − G0). Each receipt nevertheless has its own date. If payments are invested or financed at subsequent gross factors R, their terminal value is ΣnmΔGi∏j>iRj, which need not equal the telescoped sum. Never silently move an earlier cash payment to maturity.

Initial margin is collateral supporting performance; variation transfers marked gains and losses under the settlement agreement. Initial margin is not the underlying purchase price or a deductible loss. Its return, remuneration, segregation and funding must be counted. A maintenance threshold can trigger extra cash contributions. A price hedge can therefore reduce terminal price exposure while increasing near-term cash demands. Margining can reduce accumulated exposure without eliminating gap risk, operational failures or default risk.

The CME money-calculation document dated 11 June 2015 describes cash settlement variation, signed quantities and product-dependent rounding methods. Our lab deliberately uses exact arithmetic and an invented simple rule. It does not implement a current clearing rulebook, intraday call schedule or product-specific rounding convention.

Worked example 3 — A profitable quotation path can require a cash call

Hold one long contract with multiplier 50. Settlement quotations are 100, 96, 102 and 101. Deposit initial margin 400; the fictional maintenance level is 300. After each nonfinal settlement below maintenance, restore the account to 400. Gains remain in the account, which earns no interest. Close the position at the final settlement and return its balance.

Margin account in CU; the final balance is released
DateVariationBefore callContributionAfter call
0—0400400
1−200200200400
23007000700
3−506500650

Nominal variation totals 50. External cash is −400 at date 0, −200 at date 1 and +650 at date 3: also 50. Peak contributed collateral is 600, so a ring-fenced unremunerated reserve of 550, with no borrowing access, is 50 short at the first call despite the eventual gain.

If all contributions are instead borrowed and retained debt compounds at gross factors 1.01, 1.02 and 1.03 over the three intervals, final debt is 400(1.01)(1.02)(1.03) + 200(1.02)(1.03) = 634.5624. Net cash after release and repayment is 650 − 634.5624 = 15.4376. Funding costs 34.5624 relative to the 600 of principal contributed. The returned principal is not an additional trading profit. These interval gross factors are stipulated, not annual quotations that can be multiplied without a day-count conversion.

5. Why stochastic rates can separate forward and futures quotations

Work in a finite tree with strictly positive one-step pricing probabilities Q and a cash account whose next gross return Ri > 0 is known at date i. Let ZT = ∏Ri−1 be the path discount factor from 0 to T. All needed expectations exist because the tree is finite. Q must consistently price the traded assets. If those assets do not identify a unique Q, the expectations below give quotations conditional on the supplied pricing rule, rather than a uniqueness result from no arbitrage alone. For an uncollateralized terminal-only long forward with no default, its value is EQ[ZT(ST − K)]. Thus

F(0,T) = EQ[ZTST] / EQ[ZT].

For the ideal futures contract, each settlement pays Gi+1 − Gi and resets the remaining contract to zero value. Assume no fees, margin funding wedge or unsettled residual claim, and that both signs can be held. Zero value one date earlier implies EQi[(Gi+1 − Gi)/Ri] = 0. Since Ri is known at i, this is Gi = EQi[Gi+1]. The terminal fixing GM = ST and repeated conditioning give G0 = EQ[ST]. This is a finite backward induction, not an assertion that physical expectations price contracts.

G0 − F(0,T) = −CovQ(ZT, ST) / EQ[ZT].

Expand the covariance definition to obtain the difference. Deterministic path discounting makes the covariance zero, so the ideal quotations agree. Random rates alone do not fix the sign. Negative covariance of the path discount with terminal spot makes the futures quotation higher; positive covariance makes it lower. Zero covariance suffices for equality even when rates are random. The informal claim “high prices come with high rates” must be translated into this joint path-discount relationship, and it says nothing about a different collateralized contract without rederivation.

Worked example 4 — An exact two-state difference

The first gross return is 1. At date 1, states A and B have Q probabilities 1/2 each. Their next gross returns are 1.2 and 1, and their date-2 spots are known at that point to be 120 and 80. The date-1 spot prices are therefore 100 and 80, and the date-0 spot price is 90. This traded-asset process satisfies the same discounted pricing rule at every node.

The two-year bond costs (1/2)(1/1.2 + 1) = 11/12. The forward quote is 90/(11/12) = 1080/11 ≈ 98.181818. The date-1 futures quotations are 120 and 80, so the date-0 futures quotation is 100. Long-futures variation at date 1 is +20 or −20. Date-2 variation is zero because its final spot was already known in each state. Investing or financing date-1 variation leaves date-2 cash +24 or −20.

The value of this funded futures cash is (1/2)(24/1.2 − 20) = 0, although its undiscounted Q expectation at date 2 is 2. The forward's date-2 cash is 240/11 or −200/11; discounted expectation is likewise zero. Finally, Cov(Z,S) = 90 − 100(11/12) = −5/3, and −(−5/3)/(11/12) = 20/11, the observed quotation gap. Both agreements have zero initial value and different dated cash, so the quotation difference is not an arbitrage.

6. Swaps are dated exchanges, not a single notional payment

A payer-fixed interest-rate swap pays Nkαi and receives NαiLi at ti. In our basic contract the floating rate Li is fixed at ti−1 for that accrual interval and paid in arrears. The net receipt is Nαi(Li − k). The notional N is not itself exchanged in this same-currency contract. A currency swap can exchange principals in different currencies as well as coupons; those principal dates and amounts must be valued explicitly.

First suppose each floating reset is exactly the default-free deposit rate for its interval and the same funding/discount environment applies to both legs. A unit floating note just after a reset is worth one: invest that unit for the interval, receive principal plus its reset interest, use one unit to continue the rolling investment, and distribute the interest. Repeating to the final date reproduces the coupons plus return of principal. The initial note costs one, so its coupons alone are worth 1 − D(0,tn). Equivalently, define fi by 1 + αifi = D(0,ti−1)/D(0,ti); then αiDifi = Di−1 − Di, which telescopes.

Aswap = ΣαiDi > 0.
Vpayer-fixed = N[1 − Dn − kAswap].
kpar = (1 − Dn) / Aswap.

The annuity Aswap has units of years when rates are per year. N k Aswap is a CU value. This formula applies at the stipulated reset origin with D0 = 1 and no already-accrued stub. Between resets, the next floating coupon has already been fixed. Price it using that known fixing, and price later coupons from their remaining reset structure. Treating the first coupon as newly forecast can change value without changing any contractual cash.

For a more general floating index, let Di be the discount factors appropriate to the explicitly specified valuation environment. Define its payment-weighted projected rate fix by Difix = EQ[ZiLi], where the supplied consistent pricing law has EQ[Zi] = Di. This definition states exactly what price information the projection must reproduce. It is not an ordinary physical mean, and arbitrary forecasts combined with an unrelated discount curve do not establish no-arbitrage valuation.

Vpayer-fixed = NΣαiDi(fix − k).
kpar = [ΣαiDifix] / Aswap.

The simple telescoping numerator is available only when the floating projection matches the adjacent discount-ratio rates. A distinct index, tenor, credit or collateral environment can require a separate projection. One may calibrate its prices from index-linked instruments, but this chapter does not claim to construct a complete arbitrage-free joint multi-curve model from an arbitrary list of inputs.

Worked example 5 — Keep the floating projection separate from discounting

A synthetic one-million-CU swap has α = (0.5, 0.5, 1), D = (0.985, 0.965, 0.925), and payment-weighted projected annual floating rates (0.03, 0.05, 0.06). Its contractual fixed rate is 0.045. These are stipulated projected prices, not realized future fixings. The annuity is 0.4925 + 0.4825 + 0.925 = 1.9 years. Projected coupon amounts are 15,000, 25,000 and 60,000 CU; their present values are 14,775, 24,125 and 55,500, totaling 94,400 CU.

The fixed leg is 1,000,000(0.045)(1.9) = 85,500 CU. Payer-fixed value is therefore 8,900 CU, and the par rate is 0.0944/1.9 = 118/2375 ≈ 4.968421%. Replacing the supplied projection with adjacent discount ratios would give floating value 1,000,000(1 − 0.925) = 75,000, par rate 3/76 ≈ 3.947368%, and old-swap value −10,500. The 19,400-CU value difference is a change of model inputs and cash-index interpretation, not a rounding error.

For fixed projections and discounts, increasing the contractual fixed rate by one basis point reduces payer-fixed value by N Aswap(0.0001) = 190 CU. This is sensitivity to the contractual coupon. It is not a full market-rate DV01: a market curve move also changes discounts and possibly the floating projection.

7. Collateral remuneration and funding need their own ledger

Consider a deliberately narrow one-period contract paying a certain H. The holder pays its price V now, receives cash collateral equal to V from the counterparty, and can reuse that collateral without haircut or restriction to finance the purchase. At maturity the holder receives H and returns collateral V(1+c), where c is the stipulated remuneration over the period. There is no default, fee, gap, segregation or other cash requirement, and either side can enter the arrangement. Its zero-external-investment residual is H − V(1+c); no arbitrage gives V = H/(1+c). For H = 104 and c = 0.04, V = 100 and both maturity cash flows are 104.

This proof identifies why a collateral remuneration rate can determine discounting in that specific fully funded arrangement. It is not a theorem that every derivative should be discounted at an overnight curve. Different collateral currency, thresholds, independent initial margin, funding asymmetry, delayed transfer, noncash collateral, segregation or default closeout can change the cash and admissible replication. In a stochastic multi-period model those mechanisms must enter a consistent valuation argument; adding a dealer's funding spread to a discount rate without defining the arrangement is not a derivation.

For an independent segregated initial-margin amount M that must be financed externally for year fraction δ, suppose simple funding and remuneration rates are f and c. At expiry, the deposit returns M(1+cδ) while its financing requires M(1+fδ). Net funding cost is M(f−c)δ. For M = 10,000, f = 6%, c = 2% and δ = 0.25, the amounts are 10,150 owed and 10,050 returned, so the cost is 100 CU. Charging an additional 10,000 as a permanent loss would count returned principal incorrectly. Conversely, ignoring the initial liquidity requirement would miss the cash needed to open the position. This separate cost example does not mean all stochastic margin costs can be calculated from a fixed M.

8. A hedge can leave basis, quantity and liquidity risk

Define a local seller's basis at settlement as bT = Slocal,T − GT, using the actual deliverable benchmark and the same units. If a fixed quantity Q is sold locally and short futures cover exactly Q units, nominal receipts are QSlocal,T + Q(G0 − GT) = Q(G0 + bT). A fixed initial futures quote does not fix an uncertain final local basis. Delivery grade, location, sale date, quantity and fixing differences can each matter. Funding and fees must then be added with their own dates. A series of short contracts rolled to later maturities also leaves uncertain roll prices; the first quote does not lock every later contract.

A partial hedge can be preferable to matching physical units when local and benchmark price changes differ. Under the narrow objective of minimizing the variance of QΔS − hΔG, with h measured in benchmark units and ignoring financing, differentiate Q²Var(ΔS) + h²Var(ΔG) − 2QhCov(ΔS,ΔG). If Var(ΔG) > 0, the unique minimum is h* = QCov(ΔS,ΔG)/Var(ΔG); divide h* by contract size to obtain the contract count. The positive second derivative 2Var(ΔG) proves the minimum. If Var(ΔG) = 0, covariance is zero and the hedge cannot reduce this variance. Fractional h*, estimated moments, price jumps and liquidity constraints make implementation a separate decision. Minimizing variance does not automatically minimize expected cost or the probability of a missed cash call.

Reproducible cash and pricing laboratory

Download the original inputs, standard-library Python model, reference output, instructions and interpretation, and four-file integrity manifest. The model uses exact fractions and returns explicit dated carry, currency funding, finite-tree, margin, swap, collateral and basis calculations. The examples in the text can be reconstructed without the code. The model rejects malformed or out-of-scope inputs; it is a teaching implementation, not a trading, collateral or clearing system.

Before looking at the reference output, predict what happens when the two date-1 interest rates are exchanged, when maintenance margin is lowered, and when only the swap's contractual coupon changes. A correct answer must identify which other results should remain unchanged. Arithmetic reproduction is evidence that the stated model was implemented; it is not evidence that supplied market projections, funding access or contractual rights are true.

Exercises

Show dates, signs and units. Exercises 1–9 have determinate calculations or proof requirements; Exercise 10 requires an evidence-based critique. Unless a question changes an assumption, use the frictionless rights stated for the corresponding model. Attempt the questions before opening the solutions.

  1. Cash strips and old value. Spot is 72. At dates 0.25 and 0.75 the asset pays income 1.5 and 2, and incurs costs 0.4 and 0.6. The respective discounts are 0.99 and 0.96; D(0,1) = 0.92. Assume the complete carry package is reversible. Find its prepaid delivery cost, one-year forward quote and old long value at K = 76. Give the initial and dated debt ledger for selling at 76, and verify the terminal surplus and its present value.
  2. Proof and a trading-right boundary. Prove that two forwards on exactly the same deliverable and T, with strikes K1 and K2, differ in value by D(t,T)(K2 − K1) from the long holder's perspective. State the financing and closeout assumptions. Then explain why a commodity quote below a computed full-carry price need not yield an arbitrage when asset borrowing is prohibited. Identify which bound the feasible cash-and-carry trade still supplies.
  3. Currency units and executable prices. A benchmark calculation has S = 0.80 CU/FU, Dd = 0.97, Df = 0.95. Price a long 500,000-FU forward at K = 0.79. Separately, actual executable quotes are Sbid = 0.799, Sask = 0.801, foreign lending/borrowing gross factors 1.04/1.07, domestic lending/borrowing factors 1.02/1.06, and forward bid/ask 0.790/0.792. Derive both funding thresholds and determine whether either covered strategy establishes an arbitrage. Do not substitute the benchmark curves for the executable funding terms.
  4. Proportional payouts. For S = 120, T = 2, continuously compounded r = 0.01 and continuously reinvestable dividend yield q = 0.04, find F and the value of a long K = 115 forward. Derive the share-reinvestment step. Explain why F below S does not by itself identify expected depreciation and why an uncertain fixed cash dividend cannot be treated as the same q without an additional model.
  5. A stochastic-rate transfer. Modify the two-date tree: first gross is 1.02; state probabilities are (0.4,0.6), date-1 gross returns (1.25,0.95), terminal spots (160,70), with terminal spot known at date 1. Find initial spot, bond, forward and futures quotations. Derive the covariance gap and the funded terminal cash of a unit long futures. Verify its discounted value is zero. Explain the effect of replacing both second gross returns by the same positive constant.
  6. Short-side margin funding. Hold two short contracts with multiplier 25 and quotations 80,84,79,83. The total account's initial margin is 300 and maintenance is 200. Nonfinal calls restore it to 300; no funds are withdrawn before final close. The account earns zero. Borrow every contribution at consecutive interval gross factors 1.005,1.01,1.02. Construct the complete margin and debt ledger; find nominal variation, cumulative contributions, release, funding cost and net result. Would an unremunerated cash reserve of 450 alone meet the first call?
  7. Swap projection and a known fixing. Let N = 2,000,000, α = (0.5,0.5), D = (0.98,0.94), projected floating rates (0.06,0.07) and contractual fixed rate 0.065. Find the annuity, both leg values, payer-fixed value and par rate. Compute the value produced by incorrectly replacing the floating leg with N(1 − D2). Now suppose the first coupon has already fixed at 0.08 and only the second rate remains projected: revalue with the same payment dates and discounts. Explain why the contractual-coupon sensitivity is not a general market-rate DV01.
  8. Collateral is returned principal. In the one-period fully reusable collateral arrangement, H = 103 and remuneration gross is 1.02. Derive the claim value and both maturity payments. Separately, 20,000 of independent initial margin must be financed at a simple annual 5%, earns simple 1%, and is returned in half a year. Compute the two final cash amounts and net cost. Critique subtracting 20,000 as an additional loss and discounting every unrelated derivative at 2% solely because this first arrangement uses 1.02.
  9. Basis and the variance objective. A producer sells 200 local units and shorts two futures, each for 100 units, at 52. At sale, local spot is 47 and the futures fixing is 49; all measured financing costs total 150 CU. Find gross physical receipts, nominal futures receipts, final basis and total net receipts. In a separate planning model of price changes, Var(ΔS) = 9, Var(ΔG) = 16 and Cov(ΔS,ΔG) = 6. Derive the unconstrained variance-minimizing number of short contracts and compare unhedged, optimum and two-contract variances. State why the fractional optimum is not immediately an executable instruction.
  10. Research and treasury critique. An analyst writes: “The forward is the market's physical expected future spot. Futures have the same terminal difference, so their funding is irrelevant. Every floating swap leg equals one minus its final discount. A nonzero FX basis proves a free profit, and initial margin is a loss charged on top of the futures P&L.” Repair each claim using a derivation or numerical counterexample from this chapter. Use the scoped primary readings below to design a feasible validation protocol for a proposed real trade. Give a concrete data requirement, an executable-rights check, a liquidity stress and a statement of what the evidence would still not identify.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. Net income funds a dated borrowing strip

    Net receipts are 1.1 and 1.4. Their present values are 1.089 and 1.344, totaling 2.433. A = 72 − 2.433 = 69.567. Thus F = 69.567/0.92 = 69567/920 ≈ 75.616304348. Old long value at 76 is 69.567 − 69.92 = −0.353.

    At date 0 borrow 1.089 due as 1.1 at date 0.25, borrow 1.344 due as 1.4 at 0.75, and borrow 69.567 due as 69567/920 at 1. These total 72 and purchase the asset. Each interim net income pays its matched liability. Selling the forward at 76 leaves 76 − 69567/920 = 353/920 ≈ 0.383695652 at T and zero other net cash. Its PV is (353/920)(0.92) = 0.353, the negative of the old long value. Repayment dates, not only the total borrowing, establish the funded strategy.

  2. Cancel identical delivery rights

    Long the K1 contract and short the K2 contract. On T the received and delivered asset units cancel, leaving K2 − K1 CU with certainty. Buying or shorting a default-free T-dated cash claim reproduces that receipt, so vt(K1) − vt(K2) = D(t,T)(K2 − K1). If prices violate this identity, sell the more expensive cash-equivalent portfolio and buy the cheaper one, provided both positions and financing can actually be executed.

    This proof assumes matching delivery/fixing, quantity, currency, maturity, credit and settlement terms, without an asymmetric collateral or closeout cost. A forward subject to a different counterparty or collateral agreement need not have the identical net cash rights. Prohibiting short borrowing of the commodity removes the reverse cash-and-carry strategy: one cannot sell inventory today and use the cheap forward to replace it. Buying and storing the asset, financing every cost and selling a forward remains feasible under the other premises, so F cannot exceed that executable full-carry cost. It supplies an upper bound; it does not force equality or a matching lower bound. A residual convenience yield does not itself restore the missing trading right.

  3. A model value and executable thresholds answer different questions

    The benchmark F is 0.80(0.95)/0.97 = 76/97 ≈ 0.783505155 CU/FU. Long value is 500,000[0.76 − 0.79(0.97)] = −3,150 CU. The negative value says the long's fixed exchange rate is unfavorable relative to these benchmark curves; it does not establish a fundable trade at those curves.

    To sell one FU forward using actual access, acquire 1/1.04 FU now at the ask, fund its domestic cost at 1.06 and invest the foreign amount. Domestic repayment per FU delivered is (0.801/1.04)(1.06) = 42453/52000 ≈ 0.816403846. The executable forward bid 0.790 is below this upper threshold. For the reverse trade, borrow 1/1.07 FU, sell it at 0.799 and lend the domestic proceeds at 1.02. They grow to (0.799/1.07)(1.02) = 40749/53500 ≈ 0.761663551 CU. Buying one FU forward at the ask costs 0.792, more than those proceeds. Neither trade establishes an arbitrage. Fees, credit and settlement mismatches would require further checks even if one preliminary spread were favorable.

  4. Reinvestment changes share count

    Dividend receipts on n shares over dt are qnS dt. Reinvesting at price S buys qn dt shares, so n′ = qn and n(t) = n(0)eqt. Starting with e−qT shares gives one share at T, under continuous frictionless reinvestment and the specified proportional payout. Hence F = 120e−0.06 ≈ 113.011744030, and v = 120e−0.08 − 115e−0.02 ≈ −1.948885864 CU.

    The lower forward quote reflects contractual payout and funding carry. Nothing in the replication derived a physical drift or expected spot. A cash dividend that is uncertain, fixed in CU rather than proportional, or subject to a different entitlement cannot be represented by n′ = qn without an additional assumption. If q = r the formula gives F = S; if q = 0 it reduces to financing carry. Negative r is mathematically allowed while the cash account remains positive.

  5. Reconstruct the pricing law before averaging

    The path discounts are 1/(1.02·1.25) = 40/51 and 1/(1.02·0.95) = 1000/969. Their Q-weighted mean is D = 904/969 ≈ 0.932920537. Initial spot is E[ZS] = 90640/969 ≈ 93.539731682. Hence F = 11330/113 ≈ 100.265486726, G = 0.4(160) + 0.6(70) = 106, and G − F = 648/113 ≈ 5.734513274.

    Cov(Z,S) = E[ZS] − E[Z]E[S] = 90640/969 − (904/969)106 = −5184/969. Dividing its negative by 904/969 gives 648/113. Date-1 variation is 54 or −36. Its funded terminal cash is 67.5 or −34.2. Discounted value is 0.4[67.5/(1.02·1.25)] + 0.6[−34.2/(1.02·0.95)] = (0.4·54 − 0.6·36)/1.02 = 0.

    If both second gross factors equal a common positive R, path discount is constant 1/(1.02R). The two forward and futures quotations both become 106, while initial spot and bond adjust to 106/(1.02R) and 1/(1.02R). Keeping the old initial spot while changing rates and future cash would break the stipulated pricing consistency.

  6. Finance contributions, not a fictional option premium

    The signed multiplier is −2·25 = −50. Variations are −200, +250, −200, totaling −150. The account starts at 300, falls to 100 after the first variation and requires a 200 contribution; it then rises to 550 and ends at 350. Cumulative contributions are 500, and release is 350. The nominal identity 350 − 500 = −150 holds.

    Debt starts at 300, grows to 301.5 at date 1, then becomes 501.5 after funding the call. At date 2 it is 506.515. At final date it is 516.6453, equivalently 300(1.005)(1.01)(1.02) + 200(1.01)(1.02). Funding cost is 16.6453 and net cash is −166.6453. A ring-fenced 450 cash reserve leaves only 150 after the opening contribution, so it is 50 short of the first 200 call. The later increase in the account cannot pay a past obligation.

  7. A fixing is already determined cash

    A = 0.5(0.98) + 0.5(0.94) = 0.96. Floating PV is 2,000,000[0.5(0.98)(0.06) + 0.5(0.94)(0.07)] = 124,600; fixed PV is 2,000,000(0.065)(0.96) = 124,800. Payer-fixed value is −200 CU, and par rate is 0.0623/0.96 = 623/9600 ≈ 6.489583%. The inappropriate telescoping floating leg would be 120,000 and would give value −4,800, understating this stipulated model value by 4,600.

    Using the first known fixing 0.08 increases its PV by 2,000,000(0.5)(0.98)(0.02) = 19,600. Floating PV becomes 144,200 and payer-fixed value 19,400 CU. No new reset is invented. Differentiation with respect to k alone gives −N A = −1,920,000 CU per unit annual rate, or −192 CU per one basis point. It holds the two curves fixed. A market-rate move generally changes A and the floating price, so its complete value derivative requires those changes too.

  8. Specify who can use the collateral

    V = 103/1.02 = 5150/51 ≈ 100.980392157 CU. Receiving this reusable collateral finances the same initial purchase payment. At maturity the derivative pays 103 and collateral return plus remuneration is V(1.02) = 103, leaving zero under the stated arrangement. The result depends on full, reusable cash collateral and symmetric access without other costs.

    In the separate segregated-margin calculation, financing repayment is 20,000(1 + 0.05·0.5) = 20,500, while margin return is 20,000(1 + 0.01·0.5) = 20,100. Net cost is 400. The 20,000 principal creates a liquidity need but is returned, so deducting it as an additional permanent loss is incorrect. Nor is the first claim's 2% gross-rate increment a universal discounting instruction: an unrelated derivative may have a different collateral currency, remuneration, segregation, timing, credit exposure or financing arrangement. Those cash terms must be specified and priced consistently.

  9. Quantity matching can increase variance

    Physical receipts are 200(47) = 9,400. Short futures yield 2(100)(52 − 49) = 600 before financing, so gross combined cash is 10,000. Basis is 47 − 49 = −2 CU/unit; 200(52 − 2) confirms 10,000. Net cash after the stipulated 150 cost is 9,850 CU. Convergence to the benchmark deliverable's spot does not force a different local asset's basis to zero.

    In the separate variance model, h* = 200(6/16) = 75 benchmark units, or 0.75 short contracts. Unhedged variance is 200²·9 = 360,000 CU². At the continuous optimum it is 200²(9 − 36/16) = 270,000 CU². Two short contracts mean h = 200, with variance 200²(9 + 16 − 12) = 520,000 CU², which exceeds unhedged variance. The strong equal-unit hedge introduces too much benchmark variability for the covariance available.

    The unconstrained result permits fractions; actual contracts may require integers. Comparing feasible neighboring integers, checking transaction and funding costs, testing covariance stability and imposing cash limits are necessary before acting. Estimation error and a different risk objective can change the appropriate position. For example, one contract gives variance 280,000 here, but that comparison alone still omits liquidity and implementation terms.

  10. Repair inference and test the cash implementation

    The forward is fixed by relative pricing and contractual cash under stated trading rights, not by the physical expectation. A forecast needs a physical model and risk-premium reasoning. Forwards and futures have different dated cash: Worked example 4 gives different fair quotations, and Worked example 3 loses 34.5624 CU of its nominal gain to the stipulated margin funding. A floating leg telescopes only for the matched reset/discount model; Worked example 5's separate projection is worth 94,400 rather than 75,000. FX parity using inaccessible benchmark funding does not produce a trade: Worked example 2 turns its apparent 25,000 gain into a 66,080 loss when actual borrowing is specified. Initial margin is returned collateral; its net cost depends on funding, remuneration and possible losses, not a second deduction of principal.

    The primary-source roles are limited. Haugh's notes provide a route to carry and swap replication and highlight contract cash structure; the CME document supplies a dated example of settlement-variation and rounding specifications; the BIS study motivates examining hedging demand and constraints when measuring historical basis. None verifies Larch's synthetic numbers, current instrument terms or a particular firm's access.

    A feasible validation protocol freezes raw timestamped bid/ask spot, forward, rate and funding quotes; records currencies, accrual calendars, delivery and reset rights, credit and collateral terms; checks availability of both signs and actual size limits; reconstructs signed cash separately for every date; reprices each leg against independently verified inputs; and reconciles settlement rounding to the selected contract. Stress an early adverse price move, a funding spread increase, an initial-margin increase and delayed collateral return together. Require the treasury cash line to cover the largest scheduled and stressed call before treating the trade as implementable. Test projection and discount choices separately and use out-of-sample cash reconciliations rather than fitting all errors away.

    Evaluation. Award full credit for repairing all five claims, at least two correct quantitative counterexamples with dates and signs, accurate scoped use of the primary readings, an executable-rights test, a concrete joint liquidity stress, and explicit inference limits. A nonzero measured basis does not uniquely identify a causal balance-sheet mechanism; a successful historical reconciliation does not guarantee future funding; and no source substitutes for the trade's executed legal and operational terms. Alternative protocols are acceptable when they test these mechanisms and preserve reproducible evidence.

Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. Explain to a treasurer why “zero-cost hedge” is incomplete. Identify the delivery quotation, present value and dates at which cash can be required.

Model answer. A new fair forward has zero model value because its delivery price balances future rights and obligations; the asset is not being purchased for zero. A futures contract settles gains and losses before maturity, and collateral may have to be posted or replenished. A hedged eventual sale cannot finance a call that arrives first. Compute the old contract's value using its unchanged delivery price, reconcile dated variation, and include returned collateral and financing. State the assumptions under which the pricing and funding comparison holds.

Delayed retention, after 7–14 days. Without the lab: (i) with S = 60, no payout or holding cost and D = 0.96, find F and old long value at K = 61; (ii) a long futures position of multiplier 20 has successive quotation changes −3 and +5: give variations and explain why their sum alone is not a funding plan; (iii) with Aswap = 2.4, floating PV per unit notional 0.12 and N = 100,000, find the par fixed rate and value at k = 0.045; (iv) state one condition that makes the forward/futures quotations equal and one reason a physical local hedge can still leave risk.

Answers. (i) F = 62.5 and v = 60 − 61(0.96) = 1.44 CU. (ii) Variations are −60 and +100, nominal sum 40; the first 60 must be available on its earlier date, and interest and collateral cash are additional inputs. (iii) Par rate is 0.12/2.4 = 5%, and payer-fixed value is 100,000(0.12 − 0.045·2.4) = 1,200 CU. (iv) Deterministic path discounting suffices under the ideal settlement assumptions; more generally the relevant covariance can be zero. A different local grade, location, date, quantity or funding obligation can leave risk. Advancement requires all four answers, the funded ledger in a fresh short-side case, and an explanation of which claimed replication rights must be checked.

Sources and further development

Martin Haugh, Forwards, Swaps, Futures and Options (2016), Sections 1–3, is a further-study route for the financial building blocks. Our examples, finite-tree construction, proofs, exercises and laboratory are original. The two operational and empirical references are the dated CME settlement-calculation document and BIS cross-currency-basis study; neither is presented as a complete current trading specification.

The next chapter, options and binomial replication, replaces the forward's obligation with contingent exercise rights. More elaborate collateralized pricing, stochastic margin, basis dynamics and counterparty closeout require an enlarged model. The present chapter establishes the necessary discipline: define the payable cash, prove the price using attainable positions, and show how every interim payment is funded.

Sources and further study

  • Martin Haugh — Forwards, Swaps, Futures and Options (2016) — Further reading on dated carry replication, contractual forward value and swap cash decomposition; Sections1–3. Examples and exercises here are original.
  • CME Group — Money Calculations for CME-cleared Futures and Options (11 June 2015) — Dated primary specification of settlement variation, signed quantities and product-dependent rounding. The chapter uses an invented exact-arithmetic margin ledger.
  • BIS Quarterly Review — Covered interest parity lost: understanding the cross-currency basis (September2016) — Historical analysis of hedging demand and constraints on executable currency arbitrage; no current basis observation or causal identification inferred from a quote alone.
